title: Agniś ca mā: the water sipped at the evening worship
theme: At sunset the worshipper asks protection from the wrongs anger brings, names the day’s wrongs of mind, speech and body, and offers them and himself into the light that is the source of immortality.

words.context: Bhāskara: «उपक्रान्ताया रात्रेरधिपतिर् अग्निः» — the lord of the night now beginning
Sāyaṇa: «क्रोधाभिमानी देवः» — the deity of anger; Bhāskara: «मननशीलमन्तःकरणं» — the thinking inner faculty
Sāyaṇa: «क्रोधस्वामिनस्तन्नियामका देवाः» — the deities who govern anger
Sāyaṇa: «मदीयकोपनिष्पादितेभ्यः» — brought about by my anger

words.role: ablative of what one is protected from

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «अहरभिमानी देवो विनाशयतु» — the deity of the day
Sāyaṇa: «मरणरहिते जगत्कारणे» — the deathless cause of the world
Sāyaṇa: «सत्ये बाधरहिते» — the real, what is never cancelled

sandhi.rule: A visarga becomes ś before c: agniḥ + ca → agniś ca (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः), with ś by assimilation).

sandhi.type: final t voiced before a vowel

sandhi.rule: pāpam akārṣam: the m is joined to the vowel.

sandhi.type: visarga before t; final t voiced
sandhi.rule: The visarga of ahaḥ becomes s before t (ahas tad); tat before a vowel becomes tad (tad avalumpatu).
kim + ca → kiñ ca: m becomes the nasal of the following stop (P. 8.4.59 (वा पदान्तस्य)).
idam aham, mām amṛtayonau: m joined to the following vowel; aham before m is written with anusvāra.

sandhi_exceptions.note: śiśnā · ahaḥ: a daṇḍa stands between the lines and the vowels are not joined in recitation.
mayi · idam: a daṇḍa stands between the lines and the vowels are not joined.

morphology.note: Instrumental of śiśna with the Vedic ending -ā for -ena; Bhāskara names the rule: «सुपां सुलुक् इत्याकारः».
First person singular of the s-aorist of √kṛ: ‘I have done’.
manyu means anger in classical usage but has a wider older sense of spirited mind; the commentators divide on which is meant here (see commentary).

translation.literal: May Agni and manyu and the lords of manyu protect me from sins done through manyu. Whatever sin I have done by day — by mind, by speech, by the hands, by the feet, by the belly, by the sexual organ — may the day wipe that out. Whatever wrong [is] in me, this [and] myself I offer into the source of immortality, into the true, into the light. Svāhā.
translation.readable: May Fire, and anger, and the powers that rule anger guard me from the wrongs that anger brings. Whatever wrong I did today — in thought, in word, with hands or feet, by appetite or desire — may the passing day wipe it away. Whatever wrong remains in me, I offer it, and myself with it, into the source of deathlessness, the true, the light. Svāhā.

syntax: A wish in the third person imperative (rakṣantām), with three subjects joined by ca and an ablative of what is guarded against. Then a relative clause (yad … akārṣam) with six instrumentals of the means, resumed by tad and a second imperative (avalumpatu). The last sentence turns to the first person: a relative clause (yat kiṃ ca … mayi) and a main clause idam ahaṃ māṃ … juhomi with three locatives of where the offering is made.

ambiguities.note: Anger (Sāyaṇa, the anonymous commentator, and Bhāskara’s alternative) or the thinking inner faculty (Bhāskara’s first reading).

Sāyaṇa reads it as protection by removing sins already done («पापिनं मां तत्पापविनाशनेन पालयन्तु»); Bhāskara as protection from sins not yet done, ‘as one guards a house against thieves’ (see commentary).
Sāyaṇa takes idam as the collected sin and mām as the speaker in his subtle body («लिङ्गशरीररूपम्»); Bhāskara allows that mām may stand for ‘my sin’, the two being treated as one.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Bhāskara names the metres: the first two lines a three-pāda gāyatrī; the six-word list a five-pāda paṅkti of eight-syllable pādas; idam aham … juhomi a virāj or two-pāda gāyatrī. He notes seven pauses inside the mantra and that ‘akārṣam manasā’ is to be recited together. The printed lines count 16, 6, 8, 8, 7, 7, 8, 8 and 9 syllables (svāhā included in the last).

beginner: This is the prayer for sipping water at the evening worship. It first asks Fire, and anger, and the powers that govern anger, to protect the speaker from the wrongs anger leads to. Then it lists the ways a day goes wrong: in thought, in speech, with the hands, with the feet, through appetite and through desire, and asks that the day which is now ending take those wrongs away with it. Finally the speaker offers whatever wrong remains, and himself along with it, into ‘the source of deathlessness, the true, the light’. The old commentators read that last phrase as the ultimate reality, and say the water sipped is the offering. The prayer describes a review of the day; the edition makes no claim about what reciting it achieves.
analogy: Like closing the day’s accounts at sunset: each kind of entry is named, and the balance is handed over rather than carried into the night.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Agni, manyu and the lords of manyu are asked to protect the speaker from sins done through manyu. The speaker names the sin done ‘by day’ through mind, speech, hands, feet, belly and sexual organ and asks the day to wipe it out; then offers ‘whatever wrong is in me’, and himself, into the source of immortality, the true, the light, with svāhā.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: «सायंसंध्याकाले जलपानार्थं मन्त्रमाह» — the mantra for drinking water at the evening worship; the anonymous commentator says the same. Bhāskara: «पापशोधनार्थं सायम् अप आचामति» — one sips water in the evening to cleanse sin. The sins named are those ‘of the day’ because the day is ending; the morning mantra (10.32) names those of the night.

commentary.q: What is manyu, and why Agni?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa reads manyu as the deity presiding over anger and the ‘lords of manyu’ as the deities that govern it («क्रोधाभिमानी देवः», «क्रोधस्वामिनस्तन्नियामका देवाः»). Bhāskara first takes manyu as the thinking inner faculty, the cause of all action and restraint («मननशीलमन्तःकरणं सर्वप्रवृत्तिनिवृत्तिहेतुः»), and only then reports anger as another view («क्रोध इत्येके»); its lords are the breaths and the senses. Agni is named, for Bhāskara, as lord of the night that is beginning («उपक्रान्ताया रात्रेरधिपतिर् अग्निः»).

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa reads the protection as removal of sins already committed («पापिनं मां तत्पापविनाशनेन पालयन्तु»). Bhāskara reads it as guarding against sins still to come, as a house is guarded so that thieves do not enter, and paraphrases: «यथा अहं पापं न करिष्यामि तथा कुर्वन्तु». On his reading the mantra looks forward to the night as well as back over the day.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa gives an example for each: harm thought of others is the sin of the mind («परहिंसादिचिन्तनं मानसं पापम्»), unkind and untrue speech that of speech, eating what is forbidden that of the belly («अभोज्यभोजनमुदरकृतम्»), and so on. Bhāskara gives parallel examples and adds that ‘whatever wrong is in me’ covers what was done in earlier births or by the other senses («प्राचीनजन्मसञ्चितं»).

commentary.q: Into what is the offering made?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the speaker offers the collected sin, and himself as the subtle body, into the deathless cause of the world, the real, the self-luminous: «मरणरहिते जगत्कारणे सत्ये बाधरहिते ज्योतिषि स्वयंप्रकाशे वस्तुनि जुहोमि», ‘by this offering I burn it all’ («तत्सर्वं भस्मी करोमि»). Bhāskara reads ‘the source of immortality’ as Brahman («अमृतयोनौ अमृतत्वकारणे ब्रह्मणि») and the light as the self that is fire, so that the sin, losing its nature as sin, becomes a cause of immortality («पापतां हित्वा अमृतत्वस्यैव कारणं स्यादिति भावः»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The Ānandāśrama text misprints अग्रिश्च and drops a letter in पद्भ्याम्; the Tirupati e-text reads अवलिम्पतु and अमृतयोनी. All are classified as witness errors (sources page). Bhāskara’s metrical analysis is given under Metre.

advaita.text: Sāyaṇa makes the last sentence an offering of the self into Brahman understood as the world’s cause, real and self-luminous («जगत्कारणे सत्ये बाधरहिते ज्योतिषि स्वयंप्रकाशे वस्तुनि»). Reading this as an Advaita position is a modern inference: his comment does not argue for non-duality here, though the terms (real as ‘never cancelled’, self-luminous) are those Advaita uses.

schools.disagreement: No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. Between the two commentators present, Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara differ on manyu (anger, or the mind), on whether the protection is from past or future sins, and on what is offered (the sin and the subtle body, or the sin transformed into a cause of immortality).

parallels.note: The Gītā describes an offering in which the oblation and the fire are Brahman; both commentators read the ‘light’ into which the speaker offers himself as Brahman.

contemporary.text: The prayer singles out anger first, then reviews the day by the channels through which harm is done — thought, speech, hands, feet, appetite, desire. It is a structured evening review: name what happened, by what means, and let the day close on it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Of the six channels the prayer lists, which one most often carries your mistakes?
reflect.deeper: Bhāskara reads ‘protect me from sins done through manyu’ as looking forward, Sāyaṇa as looking back. Which reading makes the evening mantra more useful, and why?
reflect.practice: Tonight, recall the day once through each channel — thought, speech, action — and then deliberately set it down.

references.text: Bhāskara’s reading of the instrumental śiśnā by the rule supāṃ suluk and his analysis of the metres come from his comment on this anuvāka (his anuvāka 24).

flags.note: manyu as anger or as the thinking mind, and protection from past or from future sins, are read differently by Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara; the text does not decide.
The edition’s computed map sends Bhāskara’s anuvāka 24 to 10.32; by its content (agniś ca, sāyam) it comments on this anuvāka, and is cited here explicitly.
